summary.text: Europa is the smallest and least massive of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, and it is an icy moon.
Its surface lacks large mountains and craters, making it the smoothest known solid object in the Solar System.
A water ocean beneath the surface explains that young, smooth look and could conceivably harbor extraterrestrial life.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: Very thin, made primarily of oxygen

facts.label: Discoverers
facts.value: Simon Marius and Galileo Galilei, independently

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: NASA's Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024

items.prompt: Europa has almost no mountains or craters. What best explains its smooth, young surface?

options.label: Constant dust storms that sand everything flat
A thick atmosphere that shields it from impacts
Rock so hard that nothing can dent or crack it
An ocean of water lying beneath the surface

items.explain: The apparent youth and smoothness of the surface is due to a water ocean beneath it.

items.prompt: What does the leading model say keeps Europa's ocean from freezing?

options.label: Heat from tidal flexing as Jupiter squeezes the moon
Sunlight trapped beneath a thick blanket of air
Hot lava from volcanoes erupting under the ice
Warm currents carried in from Jupiter's atmosphere

items.explain: The predominant model says heat from tidal flexing keeps the ocean liquid.

items.prompt: Why would plumes of water vapor at Europa excite researchers hunting for life?

options.label: They would show the moon is about to break apart
They could let scientists study the ocean without landing
They would prove the moon holds a thick, rich atmosphere
They would melt the crust and reveal buried old craters

items.explain: Plume activity could help researchers search for life in the ocean without having to land on the moon.

items.prompt: Sea salt may coat some geological features on Europa. What might that suggest about the ocean?

options.label: That it is shrinking and will vanish before long
That it lies only a few meters under the ice
That it interacts with the sea floor beneath it
That it receives salt carried in from Jupiter

items.explain: Salt on the surface suggests the ocean interacts with the sea floor, which may matter for habitability.

items.prompt: Europa has one spot from which Jupiter would appear to hang directly overhead. Why does such a spot exist?

options.label: Europa is tidally locked, so one side always faces Jupiter
Its orbit passes exactly over Jupiter's two poles
Its orbit is a perfect circle, so one point stays put
Jupiter and Europa share one rotation axis and spin rate

items.explain: Europa is tidally locked, with one hemisphere constantly facing Jupiter, which creates a sub-Jovian point.

items.prompt: Europa is tidally locked to Jupiter, yet some research questions whether the lock is complete. What is the proposal?

options.label: It spins faster than it orbits, or once did
It spins slower than it orbits, and is drifting
It does not spin at all and only circles Jupiter
It spins in step with Jupiter's own daily rotation

items.explain: Research suggests tidal locking may not be full: a non-synchronous rotation has been proposed, with Europa spinning faster than it orbits, or at least doing so in the past.

paragraphs.heading: Jupiter's icy moon
paragraphs.text: Europa is the smallest and lightest of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, a bit smaller and less massive than Earth's Moon. You can spot it from Earth with ordinary binoculars. It is made mostly of silicate rock, may have an iron-nickel core, and has a very thin atmosphere that is mainly oxygen. Of the three icy Galilean moons, it orbits closest to Jupiter.

paragraphs.heading: The smoothest surface
paragraphs.text: Europa's pale surface is crossed by light tan cracks and streaks. It has no large mountains or craters, which makes it the smoothest solid object known in the Solar System. The surface is also young in geological terms. Its close orbit around Jupiter means the surface has been shaped by tidal heating.

paragraphs.heading: An ocean under the ice
paragraphs.text: Below the surface lies an ocean of water, and that ocean is why the surface looks so young and smooth. Some think the ocean could even hold life. The leading model says heat from tidal flexing keeps the water liquid and moves the ice in a way similar to plate tectonics, carrying chemicals from the surface down into the ocean. Sea salt may coat some features on the surface, a hint that the ocean is interacting with the sea floor. That could help decide whether Europa could be habitable.

paragraphs.heading: Plumes of water vapour
paragraphs.text: The Hubble Space Telescope has detected plumes of water vapour, like those seen at Saturn's moon Enceladus, thought to come from erupting cryogeysers. In May 2018, a fresh look at data from the Galileo probe, which orbited Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, backed up the plume evidence. Plumes could let researchers search for life from the hidden ocean without landing. In March 2024, though, astronomers reported that the surface may hold much less oxygen than once thought.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and name
paragraphs.text: Galileo Galilei found Europa on 8 January 1610, along with Io, Ganymede and Callisto, and Simon Marius may have found it on his own. The night before, Galileo had seen Io and Europa through his 20× telescope at the University of Padua, but could not tell them apart. Marius later named the moon after Europa, a Phoenician lover of Zeus and mother of King Minos of Crete. The names fell out of use for a long time and only returned in the mid-20th century; older books simply call it Jupiter II.

paragraphs.heading: A short, steady orbit
paragraphs.text: Europa circles Jupiter in about 3.55 days at a distance of roughly 670,900 km. Its orbit is nearly circular, with an eccentricity of only 0.009, and barely tilted. Like the other Galilean moons it is tidally locked, so one side always faces Jupiter. From one point on that side, Jupiter would seem to hang straight overhead. Some research suggests the locking may not be complete, and that Europa spins faster than it orbits, or once did.

paragraphs.heading: Visiting Europa
paragraphs.text: Spacecraft have flown past Europa since the early 1970s, but none has landed. The Galileo mission, launched in 1989, still supplies most of what is known. In September 2022 the Juno spacecraft passed within about 320 km. ESA's Juice mission, launched on 14 April 2023 to study Ganymede, will fly by Europa twice, and NASA's Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024.
